```{python}
# | echo: false
# Everything in this deck is SYNTHETIC: made-up systems and made-up runs,
# generated here from a fixed seed. The "recording" names are invented to
# look like a rig's file names, because full names in a dropdown are the
# convention this demo exists to show.
import base64

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.io as pio
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

# The "notebook" renderer defines the AMD module locally, so figures work with
# no network; "notebook_connected" points requirejs at a CDN instead.
pio.renderers.default = "notebook"
PLOTLY_CONFIG = {"displaylogo": False, "responsive": True}
BLUE, ORANGE, GREEN = "#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e", "#2ca02c"
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)


def zoom_samples(x0, dx, y, resolution):
    """meta.zoom for a long signal: the samples, compactly, for the browser.

    Stored as 16-bit integers of `resolution` units each - half the size of
    float32, and far finer than anything on screen - little-endian, base64.
    The trace itself starts empty; the plugin draws what is on screen from these.
    """
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    offset = float((y.max() + y.min()) / 2)
    stored = np.round((y - offset) / resolution)
    if np.abs(stored).max() > 32767:
        raise ValueError("resolution too fine for int16 over this signal's range")
    return {"x0": float(x0), "dx": float(dx), "dtype": "int16",
            "scale": float(resolution), "offset": offset,
            "y": base64.b64encode(stored.astype("<i2").tobytes()).decode("ascii")}
```

## What this deck shows

- **Dropdown** - pick an entry; entries are named in full
- **Slider** - an ordered parameter, one position per pre-computed value
- **Toggles** - one box per curve group, driving it on every subplot
- **Zoom** - a long signal drawn as a min/max envelope, sharpening to every
  sample as you zoom in

All four come from tags on the traces - `trace.meta` and `layout.meta` - so
they work however the figure was made. **All data here is synthetic.**

## A synthetic frequency response {.calc-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

$$H(\omega) = \frac{1/k}{1 - r^2 + 2i\zeta r}, \qquad r = \frac{\omega}{\omega_n} \tag{1}$$

$$\tilde H = H\,e^{\,\varepsilon_m + i\varepsilon_\varphi},\quad
\varepsilon_m \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.08^2),\ \varepsilon_\varphi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.05^2) \tag{2}$$

"Measured" is (2): the model (1) with noise on magnitude and phase.

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

| Synthetic recording | $f_n$ | $k$ | model |
|---|---:|---:|:--:|
| `SIM_20260913_rigA_fn42Hz_R1` | 42 Hz | 1.0 | yes |
| `SIM_20260913_rigB_fn67Hz_R1` | 67 Hz | 1.6 | yes |
| `SIM_20260913_rigC_fn31Hz_R1_nofit` | 31 Hz | 0.7 | **no** |

$\zeta \in \{0.01,\ 0.02,\ 0.05,\ 0.10\}$ on the slider.

:::
:::

The third recording has no fitted model, on purpose: its **model** toggle is
greyed out rather than offering a curve that would draw nothing.

## Frequency response explorer {.plot-slide}

```{python}
f = np.geomspace(2, 200, 700)
SYSTEMS = {
    "SIM_20260913_rigA_fn42Hz_R1": dict(fn=42.0, k=1.0, fitted=True),
    "SIM_20260913_rigB_fn67Hz_R1": dict(fn=67.0, k=1.6, fitted=True),
    "SIM_20260913_rigC_fn31Hz_R1_nofit": dict(fn=31.0, k=0.7, fitted=False),
}
ZETAS = (0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10)
DEFAULT = {"set": "SIM_20260913_rigA_fn42Hz_R1", "step": 0.02,
           "groups": ["measured", "model"]}


def response(fn, k, zeta):
    r = f / fn
    return (1.0 / k) / (1.0 - r**2 + 2j * zeta * r)


fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=1, shared_xaxes=True,
                    row_heights=[0.66, 0.34], vertical_spacing=0.05)
for name, system in SYSTEMS.items():
    for zeta in ZETAS:
        model = response(system["fn"], system["k"], zeta)
        measured = model * np.exp(rng.normal(0, 0.08, f.size)
                                  + 1j * rng.normal(0, 0.05, f.size))
        shown = name == DEFAULT["set"] and zeta == DEFAULT["step"]
        curves = [("measured", measured, dict(color=BLUE, width=1.2))]
        if system["fitted"]:
            curves.append(("model", model, dict(color=ORANGE, width=2, dash="dash")))
        for group, h, line in curves:
            tag = {"set": name, "step": zeta, "group": group}
            fig.add_scatter(x=f, y=np.abs(h), mode="lines", line=line, name=group,
                            meta=tag, visible=shown, row=1, col=1)
            # Unwrapped: above resonance the phase sits at -180 degrees, and
            # wrapped noise there flips between -180 and +180 on every sample.
            fig.add_scatter(x=f, y=np.degrees(np.unwrap(np.angle(h))), mode="lines", line=line,
                            name=group, meta=tag, visible=shown, row=2, col=1)

fig.update_xaxes(type="log", row=1, col=1)
fig.update_xaxes(type="log", title_text="Frequency [Hz]", row=2, col=1)
fig.update_yaxes(type="log", title_text="|H| [µm/N]", row=1, col=1)
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="phase [°]", range=[-190, 10], row=2, col=1)
fig.update_layout(
    height=560, showlegend=False, margin=dict(l=70, r=20, t=6, b=45),
    meta={"explorer": {
        "dropdown": "recording",
        "slider": "damping",
        "sliderFormat": "ζ = {value}",
        "toggles": True,
        "default": DEFAULT,
    }},
)
fig.show(config=PLOTLY_CONFIG)
```

::: {.plot-caption}
Dropdown: recording, named in full · slider: damping ratio · toggles drive
magnitude and phase together · drag a box to zoom, double-click to reset
:::

::: {.notes}
Switch to rigC: the model toggle greys out, because that recording has no
fitted model. The slider keeps its position across recordings - every
recording carries every damping value.
:::

## Zooming a long signal {.calc-slide}

Two synthetic run-ups: **240 000 samples each**, 120 s at 2 kHz, sweeping
5 → 50 Hz through a resonance, with a few 2 ms knocks hidden in them.

$$x(t) = A\,G\!\left(\tfrac{f(t)}{f_n}\right)\sin\varphi(t) + \varepsilon,
\qquad f(t) = 5 + 45\,\tfrac{t}{120\ \mathrm{s}} \tag{3}$$

Drawing 240 000 points on an 800-pixel plot shows nothing more than 800
columns can - so the plugin draws **one min/max pair per pixel column** for
whatever is on screen, rebuilt on every zoom:

- no peak is lost - a 2 ms knock shows at full width as a spike
- nothing is invented - it is the envelope of real samples, not a smoothing
- zoom far enough and it switches to **every sample**, and says so

The samples travel in the page as 16-bit integers with a scale (`meta.zoom`),
half the size of float32; the trace itself starts empty.

## Run-up explorer {.plot-slide}

```{python}
fs, duration = 2000.0, 120.0
t = np.arange(int(fs * duration)) / fs
f_inst = 5.0 + 45.0 * t / duration
phase = 2 * np.pi * np.cumsum(f_inst) / fs
RUNS = {
    "SIM_20260913_runup_A_R1": dict(fn=30.0, knocks=(15.0, 95.0, 110.0)),
    "SIM_20260913_runup_B_R1": dict(fn=24.0, knocks=(12.0, 88.0, 105.0)),
}
KNOCK = np.array([80.0, -60.0, 40.0, -20.0])   # 2 ms at 2 kHz

fig2 = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=1, shared_xaxes=True,
                     row_heights=[0.7, 0.3], vertical_spacing=0.05)
for name, run in RUNS.items():
    ratio = f_inst / run["fn"]
    zeta = 0.04
    gain = 1.0 / np.sqrt((1 - ratio**2) ** 2 + (2 * zeta * ratio) ** 2)
    lag = np.arctan2(2 * zeta * ratio, 1 - ratio**2)
    displacement = 12.0 * gain * np.sin(phase - lag) + rng.normal(0, 1.5, t.size)
    for when in run["knocks"]:
        i = int(when * fs)
        displacement[i:i + KNOCK.size] += KNOCK
    excitation = np.sin(phase) + rng.normal(0, 0.02, t.size)
    first = name == "SIM_20260913_runup_A_R1"
    fig2.add_scatter(x=[], y=[], mode="lines", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=1),
                     name="displacement", visible=first, row=1, col=1,
                     meta={"set": name, "group": "displacement",
                           "zoom": zoom_samples(0.0, 1 / fs, displacement, 0.01)})
    fig2.add_scatter(x=[], y=[], mode="lines", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=1),
                     name="excitation", visible=first, row=2, col=1,
                     meta={"set": name, "group": "excitation",
                           "zoom": zoom_samples(0.0, 1 / fs, excitation, 0.0001)})

fig2.update_xaxes(title_text="Time [s]", row=2, col=1)
fig2.update_yaxes(title_text="displacement [µm]", row=1, col=1)
fig2.update_yaxes(title_text="excitation [V]", row=2, col=1)
fig2.update_layout(
    height=560, showlegend=False, margin=dict(l=70, r=20, t=6, b=45),
    meta={"explorer": {"dropdown": "recording", "toggles": True}},
)
fig2.show(config=PLOTLY_CONFIG)
```

::: {.plot-caption}
Dropdown: run, named in full · toggles: channel · drag a box around a knock to
zoom · the readout says whether you are seeing an envelope or every sample
:::

::: {.notes}
Run A has knocks at 15, 95 and 110 s; run B at 12, 88 and 105 s. Each is 2 ms
wide - four samples - and still shows at full height in the whole-record
view, because a min/max envelope keeps every extreme.
:::

## Tagging your own figure

```python
fig.add_scatter(
    x=f, y=magnitude,
    meta={"set": "SIM_20260913_rigA_fn42Hz_R1",   # dropdown entry
          "step": 0.02,                           # slider position
          "group": "measured"},                   # toggle
)
fig.update_layout(meta={"explorer": {
    "dropdown": "recording", "slider": "damping",
    "sliderFormat": "ζ = {value}", "toggles": True,
    "default": {"set": "...", "step": 0.02, "groups": ["measured"]},
}})

# A long signal: empty x/y, samples in meta.zoom (base64; float32 by
# default, or int16 with a scale to halve the size)
fig.add_scatter(x=[], y=[], meta={"zoom": {
    "x0": 0.0, "dx": 1 / fs, "dtype": "int16", "scale": 0.01, "y": b64}})
```

Any tool that writes Plotly JSON can do this - the plugin reads the tags in the
browser.

## The rules it follows

- **Every dropdown entry draws** the moment it is chosen - if none of the
  ticked groups exists there, its groups are ticked instead
- **A missing curve is greyed out**, with the reason on hover, never offered
- **A missing slider position snaps** to the nearest one the entry has, and
  the readout says so
- **Controls compose** - what is visible is the intersection of all of them,
  so no control resets another
- **No peak is lost when zoomed out**, and every sample is shown when zoomed in
